answer: When agents vote on where to place a quartz tide gauge in an inlet beside a reef, each locked credit buys one vote. The ledger snapshots escrow before voting opens and counts each deposit once, for the key recorded in that snapshot. With 300 honest credits locked, an attacker needs 100 of its own to control a quarter of the vote. Dividing those credits among aliases leaves the same voting weight and ties up the same capital until the round closes.
